## GDP effects {#sec-fi-gdp}

The policies change what the government collects. The model assumes that the extra revenue is spent, in shares the
user chooses, on tax cuts, investment, current spending or transfers. Fiscal multipliers translate each use into a
change in GDP over the following years. The higher energy taxes themselves weigh on GDP too, at the excise multiplier.
The resulting change in the GDP level then feeds back into GDP growth, which drives fuel use, power demand and the
non-energy GHG drivers.

The methodology describes the multipliers in
[chapter 4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#introduction) and the feedback in
[section 4.7, GDP feedback in CPAT](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#sec-GDPFeedback). The model
follows legacy CPAT section 17, with legacy bug L24 fixed.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  R["Total revenue,<br/>scenario and baseline"] --> FS["Fiscal space fs(t)"]
  FS --> IM["Impulse imp(t)"]
  IM --> EX["Excise drag<br/>share −1"]
  IM --> US["Revenue uses<br/>pit, cit, capt, gnfs, trns"]
  M["Multipliers m_i(k),<br/>lags 0-19"] --> EX
  M --> US
  EX --> EF["GDP effect ε(t)"]
  US --> EF
  EF -- "t + 1" --> LV["GDP level lvl(t+1)"]
```

### Inputs and defaults {#sec-fi-gdp-inputs}

| Input | Code | Egypt default |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue use: labour tax cuts | `EXPLabortax` | 30% |
| Revenue use: corporate tax cuts | `EXPCIT` | 0% |
| Revenue use: public investment | `EXPCapex` | 50% |
| Revenue use: current spending (goods and services) | `EXPGoodsandserv` | 0% |
| Revenue use: targeted transfers | `EXPTransfers` | 20% |
| Multiplier source: Global, income group, Estimated or Manual | `MultipliersSource` | income group (LMIC) |
| Multiplier range: Base, Low or High | `FmAdj` | Base |
| Start year for GDP calculations | `GDPStartYear` | 2025 |
| Include endogenous GDP effects? | `GDPEndogenous` | Yes |
| Baseline real GDP growth | `gdp.base` | WEO |
| Baseline real GDP | `gdp.usd` | WEO (Egypt: 547 USD bn in 2022) |

The shares are in percent of the revenue gained.

### Fiscal multipliers {#sec-fi-multipliers}

A multiplier says by how many percent GDP responds, in the year of a fiscal change and in each later year, to a change
of a fiscal instrument by 1% of GDP. The model holds one multiplier per instrument $i$ and lag $k = 0, \dots, 19$
([A8.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-1)):

$$
m_{i}(k) = \bar{m}_{G,i}\big(\min(k, k^{last})\big) + \sigma\,s_{G,i}\big(\min(k, k^{last})\big)
$$ {#eq-fi-mult}

where

- $G$ is the multiplier group (`fis.grp`): global, the country's income group (HIC, UMIC, LMIC, LIC), the country's
  estimated table, or the manual table;
- $\bar{m}_{G,i}(k)$ is the multiplier of the group at lag $k$: for global and income groups, the median of the World
  Bank's MFMod ([methodology 4.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#income-group-specific-multipliers),
  [4.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#global-multipliers));
- $s_{G,i}(k)$ is the standard deviation of the income group, and $\sigma$ is 0 for Base, −1 for Low, +1 for High;
- $k^{last}$ is the last lag with data (11): lags 12-19 hold the lag-11 value, as in legacy.

| Source (`MultipliersSource`, first three letters) | Group used | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `Glo...` | global | MFMod medians averaged over all countries |
| `Est...` | the country's table of the legacy Multipliers tab | exact match of the country code; the income group where the country is missing, and for CIT and WAGE, whose legacy tables are empty or wrong ([methodology 4.6](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#estimated-multipliers)) |
| `Man...` | sheet Manual inputs J261:U268 | legacy addresses; lags 0-11; blank = 0 ([methodology 4.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#manual-multipliers)) |
| any other text | the country's income group | |

For Estimated and Manual, Low and High also add or subtract the income group's standard deviation, as legacy does
(issue I44).

The revenue uses map to the instruments of the multiplier tables:

| Use | Instrument | Share |
|---|---|---|
| The revenue itself (higher energy taxes) | `exc` energy excise | −1 |
| Labour tax cuts | `pit` personal income tax | `EXPLabortax` / 100 |
| Corporate tax cuts | `cit` corporate income tax | `EXPCIT` / 100 |
| Public investment | `capt` capital spending | `EXPCapex` / 100 |
| Current spending | `gnfs` goods and services | `EXPGoodsandserv` / 100 |
| Targeted transfers | `trns` transfers | `EXPTransfers` / 100 |

The tables also hold `vat` and `wage`, which no revenue use reads.

### Fiscal space {#sec-fi-fiscal-space}

The fiscal space is the revenue the scenario gains over the baseline, as a share of baseline GDP. It is total revenue:
existing taxes net of subsidies (power included), new policies, subsidy reform, producer subsidies and the methane fee
([M8.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M8-1)):

$$
rev^{fis} = rev^{net} + rev^{new} + rev^{sr} + rev^{psu} + rev^{mf}
$$ {#eq-fi-fisrev}

$$
fs_t = \frac{rev^{fis}_t - rev^{fis,B}_t}{Y^{0}_t\,M}
$$ {#eq-fi-fs}

where $rev^{fis}$ is in USD million (`fis.rev`; equal to $rev$ of @eq-fi-rtot), $rev^{fis,B}$ is that of scenario 1 in
the same year (`fis.ref`), and $fs$ is the fiscal space (`fis.sp`), share of GDP.

Lower fuel use also lowers the cost of existing subsidies (base erosion, @eq-fi-rbe), and that counts. The methane fee
counts on the scenario's own methane activity. In the baseline, $fs = 0$, so scenario 1 has no GDP effect.

### Fiscal impulse {#sec-fi-impulse}

The impulse of a year is the new revenue gain of that year: the change in the gain in USD, over this year's GDP. It is
0 before the start year of the GDP calculations:

$$
imp_t =
\begin{cases}
0 & t < t^{GDP}\\[2pt]
fs_{t} & t = t_0 \ge t^{GDP}\\[2pt]
fs_t - fs_{t-1}\,\dfrac{Y^{0}_{t-1}}{Y^{0}_t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-fi-imp}

where $t^{GDP}$ is `GDPStartYear`, $t_0$ the base year and $imp_t$ the impulse (`fis.imp`), share of GDP.

The revenue uses take the impulse only from the year the carbon price starts, as legacy does (it sets the revenue-use
shares to 0 before then):

$$
imp^{p}_t = \begin{cases} 0 & t < T^{ct}_0\\ imp_t & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-fi-impp}

where $T^{ct}_0$ is the carbon pricing start year (`CPIntro`) and $imp^{p}$ is `fis.impp`. Earlier impulses still act
through the excise drag.

Each impulse starts a cohort that acts for 20 years. The rows `fis.lag.l1` ... `fis.lag.l19` (and `fis.lagp.l1` ...
`fis.lagp.l19` for $imp^{p}$) hold the impulses of the 19 earlier years: each is the previous year's value of the row
above it, and 0 in the base year.

### GDP effect of each use {#sec-fi-effects}

The effect of each use is its share times the sum, over the 20 lags, of the impulse of that cohort times the multiplier
at that lag. The impulse of year $t$ counts at lag 0 in year $t$ ([M8.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M8-2)):

$$
eff_{exc,t} = -\sum_{k=0}^{19} imp_{t-k}\; m_{exc}(k)
$$ {#eq-fi-effexc}

$$
eff_{i,t} = \frac{sh_i}{100}\sum_{k=0}^{19} imp^{p}_{t-k}\; m_{i}(k), \qquad i \in \{pit, cit, capt, gnfs, trns\}
$$ {#eq-fi-effuse}

$$
\varepsilon_t = \mathbb{1}[\text{GDPEndogenous} = \text{Yes}]\;\Big(eff_{exc,t} + \sum_{i} eff_{i,t}\Big)
$$ {#eq-fi-eps}

where

- $sh_i$ is the revenue share of use $i$, percent;
- $eff_{i,t}$ is the GDP effect of use $i$ (`fis.eff.<i>`), share of GDP;
- $\varepsilon_t$ is the GDP effect (`gdp.eff`): the change of the GDP level against the baseline, as a share of GDP; 0
  if endogenous GDP effects are off.

The revenue itself counts as an energy tax increase: share −1 at the excise multipliers.

### GDP level and growth: the feedback {#sec-fi-feedback}

The GDP effect of year $t$ raises the level of real GDP from year $t+1$ ([M8.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M8-3)):

$$
lvl_t = \begin{cases} 1 & t = t_0 \\ 1 + \varepsilon_{t-1} & t > t_0 \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-fi-lvl}

$$
Y_t = Y^{0}_t\; lvl_t
$$ {#eq-fi-gdppos}

$$
1 + g_t = (1 + g^{0}_t)\,\frac{lvl_t}{lvl_{t-1}}, \qquad g_{t_0} = g^{0}_{t_0}
$$ {#eq-fi-growth}

where

- $lvl_t$ is the GDP level factor used this year (`gdp.lvl`);
- $Y_t$ is real GDP after the feedback (`gdp.pos.usd`), USD bn;
- $g^{0}_t$ is baseline real GDP growth (`gdp.base`) and $g_t$ real GDP growth after the feedback (`gdp.pos.pct`).

A steady effect therefore raises the level once and leaves growth unchanged afterwards; it does not compound.

Growth after the feedback is what drives demand in the year: it is computed at the very start of year $t$, before the
power and fuel-use blocks. The fuel-use block reads it raised to the income factor of the elasticities (Python
`GDPI` = $(1+g_t)^{\,inc}-1$, with $inc$ = `inc.ela.adj`), together with the demand shock factor `SHOCK`; see
@sec-demand. The road engineer model reads GDP after the feedback too (@sec-transport), and the non-energy GHG drivers
read GDP growth (@sec-emissions).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: GDP effects and feedback"}
```
# start of year t (before power and fuel use)
def gdp_start(t):
    if t == t0:
        gdp_lvl[t] = 1.0
        gdp_pos_pct[t] = gdp_base[t]
    else:
        gdp_lvl[t] = 1 + gdp_eff[t - 1]                       # last year's effect
        gdp_pos_pct[t] = (1 + gdp_base[t]) * gdp_lvl[t] / gdp_lvl[t - 1] - 1
    GDPI[t] = (1 + gdp_pos_pct[t]) ** inc_ela_adj[t] - 1      # read by fuel use

# end of year t (after revenues)
def gdp_effects(t):
    fis_rev[t] = rnet[t] + rnew[t] + rsr[t] + rpsu[t] + ch4_rev[t]
    fis_sp[t]  = (fis_rev[t] - baseline.fis_rev[t]) / (gdp_usd[t] * M_PER_BN)
    if t < GDPStartYear:
        fis_imp[t] = 0.0
    elif t == t0:
        fis_imp[t] = fis_sp[t]
    else:
        fis_imp[t] = fis_sp[t] - fis_sp[t - 1] * gdp_usd[t - 1] / gdp_usd[t]
    fis_impp[t] = 0.0 if t < CPIntro else fis_imp[t]

    group = multiplier_group(MultipliersSource, income_group)
    sign  = {'Base': 0, 'Low': -1, 'High': +1}[FmAdj]
    def m(i, k):                                  # k = 0..19, held after lag 11
        kk = min(k, 11)
        return median[group, i, kk] + sign * sd[income_group, i, kk]

    eff = {'exc': -sum(fis_imp[t - k] * m('exc', k)
                       for k in range(20) if t - k >= t0)}
    for i, share in [('pit', EXPLabortax), ('cit', EXPCIT), ('capt', EXPCapex),
                     ('gnfs', EXPGoodsandserv), ('trns', EXPTransfers)]:
        eff[i] = share / 100 * sum(fis_impp[t - k] * m(i, k)
                                   for k in range(20) if t - k >= t0)
    gdp_eff[t] = sum(eff.values()) if GDPEndogenous == 'Yes' else 0.0
    gdp_pos_usd[t] = gdp_usd[t] * gdp_lvl[t]
```
:::

### The timing rule {#sec-fi-timing}

**Revenue of year $t$ changes GDP only from year $t+1$.** GDP growth after the feedback reads the level of the
current year, which holds the effect of the previous year. The rule has three consequences, kept as rules of the
model:

1. The fiscal space of year $t$ reads revenue of year $t$ only: no later year, no lookup over a whole row.
2. A same-year GDP effect never reaches same-year demand. The impulse of year $t$ counts at lag 0 in $\varepsilon_t$,
   which acts on GDP from $t+1$.
3. No other block reads a later year. With this lag, no revenue line can close a circular reference, whatever it reads
   (fuel use, power, methane).

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  a1["Year t: GDP level<br/>1 + ε(t−1)"] --> b1["Year t: power,<br/>fuel use"] --> c1["Year t:<br/>revenues"] --> d1["Year t: fiscal space,<br/>impulse, ε(t)"]
  d1 --> a2["Year t+1: GDP level<br/>1 + ε(t)"] --> b2["Year t+1: power,<br/>fuel use"]
```

This lag is what makes the whole model computable year by year: GDP growth depends only on earlier years.

### Memo rows {#sec-fi-gdp-memo}

Three memo rows report the GDP effects in other forms.

**Contribution of each use to GDP growth.** The change in the use's effect over the previous year, on the level:

$$
gdpg_{i,t} = \mathbb{1}[\text{GDPEndogenous} = \text{Yes}]\;(1 + g^{0}_t)\,\frac{eff_{i,t-1} - eff_{i,t-2}}{lvl_{t-1}}
$$ {#eq-fi-gdpg}

with $eff_{i,t-2} = 0$ in the first projection year and $gdpg = 0$ in the base year. The total $gdpg_{all}$ uses
$\varepsilon$ in place of $eff_i$ and equals $g_t - g^{0}_t$: the channels sum to it.

**Year of the reform.** $gdpy_t = t - t^{GDP} + 1$. The growth effect of reform year $N$ is $gdpg_{all}$ in the year
where $gdpy = N$.

**Change in real GDP.** $\Delta Y_t = Y_t - Y^{0}_t$ (`gdp.chg.usd`), USD bn.

| Row | Content | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `fis.rev`, `fis.ref` | Total revenue of the scenario and of scenario 1 (@eq-fi-fisrev) | USD m |
| `fis.sp` | Fiscal space (@eq-fi-fs) | share of GDP |
| `fis.imp`, `fis.impp` | Impulse; impulse used by the revenue uses (@eq-fi-imp, @eq-fi-impp) | share of GDP |
| `fis.lag.l1`-`l19`, `fis.lagp.l1`-`l19` | Impulses 1 to 19 years back | share of GDP |
| `fis.grp`, `fis.key` | Multiplier group; key (group, range) into sheet Multipliers | text |
| `fis.eff.<i>` | GDP effect of each use and of the excise drag (@eq-fi-effexc, @eq-fi-effuse) | share of GDP |
| `gdp.eff` | GDP effect (@eq-fi-eps) | share of GDP |
| `gdp.lvl` | GDP level factor (@eq-fi-lvl) | factor |
| `gdp.pos.usd` | Real GDP after the feedback (@eq-fi-gdppos) | USD bn |
| `gdp.pos.pct` | Real GDP growth after the feedback (@eq-fi-growth) | % |
| `gdpg.<i>`, `gdpg.all` | Contribution to GDP growth (@eq-fi-gdpg) | share |
| `gdpy` | Year of the reform | number |
| `gdp.chg.usd` | Change in real GDP against the baseline | USD bn |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 16 "GDP effects and external balance" (`fis.*`, `gdp.*`, `gdpg`, `gdpy`), with
  `gdp.pos.pct` in the header (section 0). Inputs on ScenarioDefinition: `EXPLabortax`, `EXPCIT`, `EXPCapex`,
  `EXPGoodsandserv`, `EXPTransfers`, `MultipliersSource` (row 226), `GDPStartYear` (row 236), `FmAdj` (row 263),
  `GDPEndogenous`. Multipliers on sheet Multipliers (from the legacy sheet: MFMod medians and standard deviations by
  group, instrument and lag), looked up by `fis.key` & instrument in `MultVal`; manual multipliers on sheet Manual
  inputs J261:U268. The lag rows are "previous column of the row above".
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/gdp.py`: `start()` at the start of the year (equation M8.3; also `GDPI`,
  `SHOCK`), `effects()` at the end (M8.1, M8.2), `multipliers()` (A8.1, tables `mult_mfmod_median_<group>`,
  `mult_mfmod_sd_<group>`). In the chain, `gdp.start` is the first block of the year and `gdp.effects` follows the
  revenues (`chain.py`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT and from the methodology"}
- **L24 fixed (LD54):** the effect raises the GDP level once, one year later ($lvl_t = 1 + \varepsilon_{t-1}$). Legacy
  adds the effect to the growth rate every year, so a steady effect compounds. The one-year lag also avoids a circular
  reference (revenue depends on fuel use, which depends on growth).
- **Revenue (LD55), as legacy:** total revenue (legacy's `rev.new.usd`, row 8026, the total of all instruments), not
  new-policy revenue only. The methane fee counts on the scenario's own activity, as legacy (issue I47). Before the
  revenue was summed from its parts, a form `rtot − rmf` still referenced the methane fee and LibreOffice reported a
  circular reference (Err:522) on a full recalculation: the fiscal revenue is therefore written as the sum of its parts
  (@eq-fi-fisrev).
- **Impulse and start year, as legacy** (legacy row 14356; issues I41, I42). The revenue uses take the impulse only
  from `CPIntro`, as legacy sets the revenue-use shares to 0 before then (issue I43); earlier impulses count only as an
  excise drag (tiny for Egypt).
- **Multipliers (LD56), as legacy:** Global, income group, Estimated or Manual; Base, Low and High with the income
  group's standard deviation (I44). Legacy bug L76 fixed: legacy's CIT table is empty, WAGE reads the GNFS table, the
  country match is approximate and the source defaults to Estimated.
- **Legacy bugs fixed:** L68 (legacy applies the lag-1 multiplier in the impulse year; here lag 0 acts in the impulse
  year), L69 (the first cohort's excise drag is lost).
- **Scenario-1 lookups stop at the current year**, which avoids a circular reference with the GDP feedback. Values are
  unchanged.
- **Methodology ([section 4.7](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#sec-GDPFeedback)).** The section
  was added to the methodology on 2026-10-31 (correction DOC1) and follows this model: fiscal space on total revenue
  (as legacy), the impulse scaled by the GDP ratio $Y^{0}_{t-1}/Y^{0}_t$, from `GDPStartYear`, the revenue uses from
  `CPIntro`, and the same feedback equations (@eq-fi-lvl, @eq-fi-growth).
- **CPAT Python:** the Estimated and Manual multiplier sources are not implemented yet (`multipliers()` raises
  `NotImplementedError`); Global and the income groups are.
- **Memo rows:** legacy rows 16166-16175 add the effects to growth every year (L24), so its channel contributions are
  not comparable with `gdpg`. Legacy shifts a row to later columns for the year of the reform; that row read forward
  through the GDP chain and made a circular reference, so `gdpy` is a number row instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: results for Egypt"}
Scenario 2 of the shipped file:

| | 2027 | 2030 | 2035 | 2040 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fiscal space (share of GDP) | 0.74% | 0.75% | 0.65% | 0.57% |
| GDP effect (level) | 0.00% | −0.02% | 0.17% | 0.39% |

The fiscal space jumps to about 0.75% of GDP when the policies start. With new-policy revenue only, as in earlier
versions, it was 0.55% in 2030. The revenue first lowers GDP: the excise multiplier peaks two years after the impulse.
From the early 2030s public investment and transfers outweigh it, and GDP ends about 0.4% above the baseline. The
effect raises fuel use a little through the income elasticities.

**Legacy benchmark.** The legacy file without proprietary data sets the baseline GDP-effect rows to 0, but its policy
rows 14584-14607 hold the cached values of a carbon-tax run: GDP effect −0.07% in 2030, +0.34% in 2035, +1.22% in
2040. Its carbon price rises to about 175 USD/t in 2041, so it is not the prototype's scenario. The comparison is
therefore against an independent Python recomputation that iterates the whole model on the growth path until it
converges; growth depends only on earlier years. A second benchmark is legacy's cached Egypt policy run (carbon tax 0
to 5 USD/t, linear 2026-2040): compare $\varepsilon$ (`gdp.eff`) with legacy row 14592 and the fiscal space with row
14336, not GDP growth (which differs because of L24).
:::

## External balance {#sec-fi-external}

Lower fossil fuel use means lower imports, or more exports, of oil, gas and coal. Block 16b values the change in fuel
use at the supply price and scales it by the share of each fuel group that is traded, then adds it to the energy trade
balance and to the current account of the baseline. All rows are in USD bn, real
([A8.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-2)).

### Trade data {#sec-fi-trade-data}

For each trade group $g$ (oil products, gas, coal) the base-year energy balance gives imports $M_g$, production $P_g$
and exports $X_g$ (exports are negative in the balance). From them:

$$
ts_g = \frac{M_g - X_g}{M_g + P_g - X_g} \quad (1 \text{ where the denominator is } 0)
$$ {#eq-fi-ts}

$$
TB_{g,t} = -(M_g + X_g)\,\theta\,\frac{p^{int}_{g,t}}{u_g}\,\frac{1}{M}
$$ {#eq-fi-tb}

where

- $ts_g$ is the share traded of the group (`ts_<group>`); Egypt: gas 0.19, oil products 0.47, coal 1.0;
- $TB_{g,t}$ is the baseline energy trade balance, exports minus imports (`xtb.<group>`);
- $p^{int}_{g,t}$ is the real international price of scenario 1's price source (oil per barrel, gas per MMBtu on the
  country's gas market, coal per tonne), and $u_g$ the GJ per unit (6.12 GJ per barrel, 1.055056 GJ per MMBtu, 25.14 GJ
  per tonne).

The oil group holds gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, jet fuel and other oil products.

### Change in net imports {#sec-fi-xnim}

For each fossil fuel, the change in use against the baseline is valued at the supply price and scaled by the share
traded of its group:

$$
\Delta NIM_{f,t} = \Delta F_{f,t}\;\theta\;sp_{f,t}\;ts_{g(f)}\;\frac{1}{M}
$$ {#eq-fi-xnim}

where

- $\Delta F_{f,t}$ is the change in total use of the fuel against scenario 1 (`echg`, block 11b, @sec-demand), ktoe;
- $sp_{f,t}$ is the supply price (`sp`, @sec-prices), USD/GJ;
- $\Delta NIM_{f,t}$ is the change in net energy imports (`xnim.<fuel>`), positive for more imports.

| Fuel | Supply price used | Trade group |
|---|---|---|
| Coal | industry supply price of coal | coal |
| Natural gas | industry supply price of gas | gas |
| Jet fuel | kerosene | oil |
| Gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, other oil products | the fuel's own price | oil |

The fuel rows are summed by group (`xnim.grp.oil`, `.nga`, `.coa`) and in total (`xnim.all`).

### Trade balance and current account {#sec-fi-ca}

The scenario's energy trade balance is the baseline balance less the change in net imports:

$$
TB^{P}_t = \sum_g TB_{g,t} - \sum_f \Delta NIM_{f,t}
$$ {#eq-fi-xtbp}

Both, and the change in net imports, are also given as shares of baseline real GDP (`xtb.pct` = $TB^P/Y^0$,
`xnim.pct` = $\Delta NIM/Y^0$; 0 where GDP is 0).

The current account starts from the WEO series and adds the change in net imports, in USD and in percent of GDP:

$$
\begin{aligned}
CA^{r}_t &= CA_t\,\nu_t && \text{real current account, pre-policy }(\texttt{bca.r})\\
\Delta CA_{g,t} &= -\Delta NIM_{g,t} && \text{change by fuel group }(\texttt{bca.d})\\
CA^{P}_t &= CA^{r}_t + \textstyle\sum_g \Delta CA_{g,t} && \text{after the policy }(\texttt{bca.p})\\
\hat{Y}_t &= \left|CA^{r}_t / ca_t\right| && \text{implied GDP / 100 }(\texttt{bca.y}\text{; 0 if }ca_t = 0)\\
ca^{P}_t &= ca_t + \textstyle\sum_g \Delta CA_{g,t} / \hat{Y}_t && \text{after the policy, percent of GDP }(\texttt{bca.pp})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fi-bca}

where

- $CA_t$ is the current account balance (WEO `BCA`, `bca`), USD bn nominal, held after its last data year;
- $ca_t$ is the current account in percent of GDP (WEO `BCA_NGDPD`, `bca.gdp`), held likewise;
- $\nu_t$ is the US CPI index (`infl`, 1 in the results year);
- `bca.dp.<group>` = $\Delta CA_{g,t}/\hat{Y}_t$; the memo `bca.n` is the current account in current prices, 0 after
  the last data year.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: external balance"}
```
for t in years:
    for f, g in [('coa', 'coa'), ('nga', 'nga'), ('gso', 'oil'), ('die', 'oil'),
                 ('lpg', 'oil'), ('ker', 'oil'), ('jfu', 'oil'), ('oop', 'oil')]:
        if f in ('coa', 'nga'):
            price = sp['ind', f, t]
        else:
            price = sp['all', 'ker' if f == 'jfu' else f, t]
        xnim[f, t] = echg[f, t] * PJ_PER_KTOE * price * ts[g] / M_PER_BN
    for g in ['oil', 'nga', 'coa']:
        xnim_grp[g, t] = sum(xnim[f, t] for f in fuels_of(g))
        xtb[g, t] = -(imports[g] + exports[g]) * PJ_PER_KTOE / M_PER_BN \
                    * p_int[g, t] / gj_per_unit[g]
    xnim_all[t] = sum(xnim_grp[g, t] for g in groups)
    xtbp[t]     = sum(xtb[g, t] for g in groups) - xnim_all[t]
    xtb_pct[t]  = safe_div(xtbp[t], gdp_usd[t])
    xnim_pct[t] = safe_div(xnim_all[t], gdp_usd[t])

    bca_r[t] = bca[t] * infl[t]
    bca_p[t] = bca_r[t] - sum(xnim_grp[g, t] for g in groups)
    bca_y[t] = abs(bca_r[t] / bca_gdp[t]) if bca_gdp[t] != 0 else 0.0
    bca_pp[t] = bca_gdp[t] + sum(safe_div(-xnim_grp[g, t], bca_y[t]) for g in groups)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, block 16b inside section 16 (`xnim`, `xtb`, `xtbp`, `xtb.pct`, `xnim.pct`, `bca*`).
  The share traded and the trade balance are data on sheet WEO (keys `<country>|ts_<group>`, `<country>|tb_<group>`,
  from the data step `extract_gdp`; legacy Mitigation rows 741-743); the current account is typed for Egypt
  (`bca`, `bca_gdp`, `bca_n`; other countries 0).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/gdp.py`, `trade_data()` (share traded and trade balance from the energy
  balance and the international prices; WEO current account for any country) and `external()` (equation A8.2).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **L49 fixed:** legacy leaves the share traded out for oil, so its oil effect is about twice as large.
- **L50 fixed:** legacy's balance-of-payments panel (rows 18160-18204) has a pre-policy current account of `#NAME?`
  (stale WEO codes), rows that lag one column (it shows the 2021 balance, −5.85, in 2022), and a sign of the policy
  net imports that looks reversed.
- **L214 fixed:** legacy's current account after the policy in % of GDP leaves coal out.
- **L215 not replicated:** legacy values the gas import bill with a unit error (USD per MMBtu on GJ); here every fuel is
  valued at its supply price in USD/GJ.
- **As legacy:** the implied GDP of the % of GDP rows (issue I129); the current account in current prices is 0 after
  the last data year (issue I130).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: results for Egypt"}
Carbon tax of 20 USD, 2030: change in net imports −1.2 bn USD, of which oil −0.93 bn. Baseline energy trade balance
2022: −6.7 bn USD.
:::

## Carbon pricing indicators {#sec-fi-carbon-pricing}

How heavily is carbon priced, once every tax and subsidy on energy is counted? Section 17 answers with revenue per
tonne of CO2, by fuel and for the economy, and with the share of emissions the new carbon tax and ETS cover
([A7.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A7-5)). The methodology discusses coverage in
[section 3.9.3.1.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#policy-coverage-and-exemptions).

### Implicit carbon price and effective carbon rate {#sec-fi-tcp}

**Implicit carbon price by fuel.** The revenue net of subsidies of the fuel, final use and power generation, divided by
its CO2:

$$
tcp_f = \frac{rfu_f + rfg_f}{CO2_f}, \qquad
tcp_{all} = \frac{\sum_{f \in \text{fossil}} rfu_f + \sum_{k \in \{coal,gas,oil\}} rfg_k}{CO2}
$$ {#eq-fi-tcp}

where $CO2_f$ is the CO2 of the fuel (power included; @sec-emissions), MtCO2, $rfg_f$ applies to coal, gas and other
oil products only, and $tcp$ is in USD/tCO2 (`tcp`; 0 where the CO2 is 0). Biomass is left out: it has no CO2.

This is the tax-and-subsidy wedge per GJ divided by the emission factor. A carbon tax of $\tau$ USD/t raises every fuel's
implicit price by about $\tau$.

**Effective carbon rate.** All revenue net of subsidies, per tonne of energy CO2:

$$
ecr = \frac{rev^{net} + rev^{new} + rev^{sr}}{CO2}
$$ {#eq-fi-ecr}

so VAT, the electricity subsidy gap and electricity VAT count. `ecr` is the summary row of section 17.

### Coverage {#sec-fi-coverage}

**CO2 covered by the new carbon tax** in each of the 17 coverage sectors $e$ (power and the 16 subsectors): the CO2 of
the fuels whose coverage switch is on, counted only where the sector's carbon tax rate is above 0:

$$
CO2^{cov}_e = \mathbb{1}[ct_e > 0]\sum_{f} CO2_{e,f}\;\kappa^{ct}_f
$$ {#eq-fi-covct}

where $\kappa^{ct}_f$ is the fuel's carbon tax coverage switch (`ctcov`). Power uses the CO2 of coal, gas and oil
generation. A sector in a non-complementary ETS has a carbon tax rate of 0 and so no covered CO2.

**Coverage shares and effective carbon tax:**

$$
cov^{ct}_G = \frac{\sum_{e \in G} CO2^{cov}_e}{CO2}, \qquad
cov^{ets} = \frac{CO2^{ets}}{CO2}, \qquad
cov = cov^{ct}_{all} + cov^{ets}, \qquad
p^{eff} = \tau\;cov^{ct}_{all}
$$ {#eq-fi-cov}

where $G$ is a sector group (transport, buildings, industry, other energy use, power) or all sectors, $CO2^{ets}$ the
CO2 covered by the new ETS (`co2.ets`, @sec-emissions), $\tau$ the carbon price (`cptraj`) and $p^{eff}$ the effective
carbon tax (`cpeff`), USD/tCO2.

| Row | Content | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp.<fuel>`, `tcp.all` | Implicit carbon price (@eq-fi-tcp) | USD/tCO2 |
| `ecr` | Effective carbon rate (@eq-fi-ecr); summary row | USD/tCO2 |
| `covct.<sector>` | CO2 covered by the new carbon tax (@eq-fi-covct) | MtCO2 |
| `cov.ct.<group>`, `cov.ct.all` | Shares of energy CO2 covered by the carbon tax | % |
| `cov.ets` | Share covered by the new ETS | % |
| `cov.all` | Covered by the carbon tax or the ETS | % |
| `cpeff` | Effective carbon tax (@eq-fi-cov) | USD/tCO2 |

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: carbon pricing indicators"}
```
for t in years:
    for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'gso', 'die', 'lpg', 'ker', 'jfu', 'oop']:
        rev = rfu[f, t] + (rfg[f, t] if f in ('coa', 'nga', 'oop') else 0.0)
        tcp[f, t] = rev / co2[f, t] if co2[f, t] != 0 else 0.0
    rev_all = sum(rfu[f, t] for f in fossil) \
              + sum(rfg[k, t] for k in ('coa', 'nga', 'oop'))
    tcp['all', t] = safe_div(rev_all, co2_all[t])
    for g in groups + ['pow']:
        cov_ct[g, t] = safe_div(sum(covct[e, t] for e in sectors_of(g)), co2_all[t])
    cov_ct['all', t] = safe_div(sum(covct[e, t] for e in coverage_sectors), co2_all[t])
    cov_ets[t] = safe_div(co2_ets[t], co2_all[t])
    cov_all[t] = cov_ct['all', t] + cov_ets[t]
    cpeff[t]   = cptraj[t] * cov_ct['all', t]
    ecr[t]     = safe_div(rnet[t] + rnew['all', t] + rsr['all', t], co2_all[t])
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 17 (`tcp`, `cpeff`, `covct`, `cov.ct`, `cov.ets`, `cov.all`, `ecr`); the
  shares call `SAFEDIV` and `SCALEBY` in the LAMBDA column.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/emissions.py`, `carbon_pricing()` (equation A7.5); `covct` is computed with
  the report by instrument in `totals.revenues()`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **Implicit carbon price:** legacy's "total carbon price" by fuel (F5d). Biomass is left out; legacy gives `#DIV/0!`.
- **Effective carbon rate** (legacy row 16662), as legacy: VAT, the electricity subsidy gap and electricity VAT count.
  The OECD's effective carbon rate counts carbon taxes, excises and permit prices only (issue I36).
- **Coverage** shares as legacy rows 16152-16157; the effective carbon tax as legacy row 16137.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: results for Egypt"}
Implicit carbon price in 2022 (subsidies make it negative): gas −151, diesel −249, LPG −280, all fossil fuels −179
USD/tCO2. A carbon tax of 20 USD raises every fuel by about 20.

Effective carbon rate 2022: −207 USD/tCO2 (legacy −122; the price data differ).

Coverage of the carbon tax, carbon tax scenario, 2030: 99.8% of energy CO2 (legacy 98.8%), of which power 41%.
:::

## Welfare and externalities {#sec-fi-welfare}

Section 18 puts a money value on what the policy does to society. It values climate damages at the social cost of
carbon, air pollution and road transport externalities with the inputs of the two co-benefit modules, and efficiency
(deadweight) costs with the tax wedges. From the same building blocks it computes fossil fuel subsidies, explicit and
implicit, and efficient prices. The methodology describes the framework in
[section 3.7, Monetized social costs and benefits](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#monetized-social-costs-and-benefits).

Results are in USD bn, real, unless stated.

### Social cost of carbon {#sec-fi-scc}

The social cost of carbon (SCC) values a tonne of CO2. The model offers five paths and picks one for the national
value and one for the global value ([M1.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-6)):

$$
\begin{aligned}
SCC^{tgt}_t &= SCC^{*}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - T^{*}}\\
SCC^{Rn}_t &= SCC^{R}_{c}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}, \qquad SCC^{Rg}_t = SCC^{R}_{world}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}\\
SCC^{EPA}_t &= SCC^{EPA}\,(1 + g^{scc})^{\,t - t_0}\\
SCC^{man}_t &= \text{manual path}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fi-scc}

where $SCC^{R}_c$ is the national value of Ricke et al. (2018) for the chosen pure rate of time preference and
elasticity of marginal utility (sheet SCC, key `<country>.<rate>.<elasticity>`), $SCC^{R}_{world}$ the global value
(key `wld.<rate>.<elasticity>`), and $t_0$ the base year. The national SCC ($SCC^{nat}$, `scc.nat`) and the global SCC
($SCC^{glo}$, `scc.glo`) take the path chosen by `NSCCSrc` and `GSCCSrc` (first letter: T, R, M, U or E).

| Setting | Code | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Target-consistent price $SCC^{*}$ | `SCCTgt` | 75 USD/tCO2, real |
| Its year $T^{*}$ | `SCCTgtYr` | 2030 |
| Real growth $g^{scc}$ | `SCCGr` | 4% a year |
| National and global SCC source | `NSCCSrc`, `GSCCSrc` | Target (choices: Target, Ricke, Manual, EPA) |
| Ricke et al. (2018) settings | | pure rate of time preference 2, elasticity 1.5 |
| US EPA SCC in the base year | | 62 USD/tCO2 |
| Manual path | Manual inputs row 237 | |

**Climate cost per GJ** of each fossil fuel, with the generic CO2 factor of the fuel (not calibrated):

$$
cc^{nat}_f = SCC^{nat}\,EF_f, \qquad cc^{glo}_f = SCC^{glo}\,EF_f
$$ {#eq-fi-cc}

for coal, gas, other oil products, gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, where $EF_f$ is the generic emission factor
(tCO2/GJ) and $cc$ is in USD/GJ (`cc.nat`, `cc.glo`).

### Climate damages {#sec-fi-climate}

Climate damages are the SCC times GHG emissions excluding LULUCF (@sec-emissions); the welfare gain is the damage
avoided against the baseline:

$$
D^{x} = \frac{SCC^{x}\;GHG}{M}, \qquad W^{cli,x} = D^{x,B} - D^{x}, \qquad x \in \{nat, glo\}
$$ {#eq-fi-dmg}

where $GHG$ is in Mt CO2e, $D$ the climate damage (`dmg.nat`, `dmg.glo`) and $W^{cli}$ the damage avoided (`wcli.nat`,
`wcli.glo`), USD bn.

### Efficiency costs {#sec-fi-efficiency}

A tax or subsidy drives a wedge between what users pay and what supply costs. When a policy changes fuel use, the
welfare cost is the wedge times the change in use: a Harberger triangle plus, with a prior tax, a rectangle
([methodology 3.7.1.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#efficiency-costs-in-cpat)). The model takes
the average of the wedges of the scenario and the baseline (a trapezoid).

**The wedge** is revenue net of subsidies per unit of use:

$$
w_f = \frac{rfu_f + rfg_f}{F_f}, \qquad w_{ecy} = \frac{rfu_{ecy}}{F_{ecy}}
$$ {#eq-fi-wdg}

where $F_f$ is total use of the fuel (`ener`, section 11), $F_{ecy}$ electricity demand (`eldem`), both ktoe, $rfg$
applies to coal, gas, other oil products and biomass, and $w$ is in USD million per ktoe (`wdg`; 0 where use is 0).

**The efficiency cost** of each fuel (biomass and the power fuels included) and of electricity:

$$
EC_f = -\,\frac{w_f + w^{B}_f}{2}\;\frac{\Delta F_f}{M}, \qquad EC = \sum_f EC_f + EC_{ecy}
$$ {#eq-fi-eff}

where $\Delta F_f$ is the change in use against the baseline (`echg`; electricity: `eldem` − `eldem`$^B$) and $EC$ is
the efficiency cost (`eff`), USD bn: positive is a cost. With subsidies (negative wedges), a fall in use is a gain.

**Efficiency cost of the methane fee.** For each methane source $j$ (oil and gas upstream, downstream gas, coal mines,
biomass, livestock, rice, waste), the abatement curve gives the abated share $a_j\,p^{b_j}$ at a fee $p$ per tonne of
CH4. The fee used on the curve is capped where abatement reaches 1:

$$
p^{mf}_j = \begin{cases} 0 & a_j = 0\\ \min\!\left(m\,GWP_j\,\delta^{mf}_j,\ a_j^{-1/b_j}\right) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-fi-mfp}

$$
MC_j = E^{0}_j\,\frac{Act_j}{Act^{0}_j}\;abt_j\;p^{mf}_j\;\frac{b_j}{1+b_j}\;\frac{1}{10^{6}}, \qquad MC = \sum_j MC_j
$$ {#eq-fi-mfc}

where

- $m$ is the methane fee (`mfee`), USD/tCO2e, $GWP_j$ the global warming potential and $\delta^{mf}_j$ 1 if the fee
  applies to the source;
- $a_j$, $b_j$ are the parameters of the abatement curve (country, else average); where $b_j = 0$ or the cap
  overflows, there is no cap;
- $E^{0}_j$ is the source's emissions in the inventory year (kt CH4), $Act_j / Act^{0}_j$ its activity against the base
  year, and $abt_j$ its abated share (@sec-emissions);
- $p^{mf}_j$ is `mfp` (USD/tCH4) and $MC$ the methane fee cost (`mfc`), USD bn: the area under the abatement curve.

### Air pollution costs {#sec-fi-airpol}

The air pollution module provides two things (@sec-emissions gives the pollutant emissions it reads): the marginal
damage of each fuel in each subsector, and the value of a change in modelled PM2.5 concentration
([A8.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-3)). The methodology describes the economic valuation in
[chapter 6, section 6.7](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/06_Air_pollution.html#sec-eco_ap).

**Cost per unit of fuel, by price code.** The marginal damage per GJ of each subsector (`airpol.mc`, computed before the
year loop with the Pigouvian taxes, [A1.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A1-2)) is averaged over the subsectors of the price
code, weighted by the scenario's own fuel use of the year:

$$
ap_{c} = u_c\;\frac{\sum_{s \in c} mc^{ap}_{s,f}\,F_{s,f}}{\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}}
\quad \Big(\text{the plain average where } \textstyle\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f} = 0\Big)
$$ {#eq-fi-apc}

where $u_c$ is the GJ per price unit (litres for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene; 1 for coal, gas and other oil
products, which are in USD/GJ) and $ap_c$ is `airpol.cost`. The price codes are coal and gas for industry, residential
(buildings subsectors) and power (the plant's own value), the four road and household oil products over all oil-using
subsectors, and other oil products for power and industry. Per GJ, $ap^{gj}_c = ap_c / u_c$ (`airpol.cost.gj`).
Residential coal counts only where buildings' coal use exceeds `ApCoalResMin` (0.1%) of buildings' total fuel use.

**Averages for other uses** (block 18), weighted by the use of the year (`apq`): coal and gas "other" average industry,
residential (buildings use) and power (power fuel use); "other oil and diesel" (`odo`) averages diesel in transport and
other oil products in power and industry (0 where all three are 0); `oop.avg` averages other oil products in power and
industry.

**Air pollution cost of electricity** (memo), USD/kWh:

$$
ap_{ecy} = \frac{\sum_{k \in \{coal, gas, oil\}} ap^{gj}_{pow,k}\;PE_k\;\theta}{G^{tot}\,H}
$$ {#eq-fi-apecy}

**Modelled PM2.5 concentration** by module source $m$ (coal, gas and other power plants, road, ground level, other,
food), from the pollutant emissions of section 15:

$$
PM_m = 1000 \sum_p AP_{m,p}\;\kappa_{m,p}, \qquad PM = \sum_m PM_m
$$ {#eq-fi-pm}

where $AP_{m,p}$ is the emission of pollutant $p$ by source $m$ (`aps`), kt, $\kappa_{m,p}$ the module's concentration
coefficient (µg/m³ per t; NOx, SO2, BC, POM, other PM, VOC, CH4, CO, PM2.5, OC) and $PM$ the modelled ambient PM2.5
(`air.con.pm2.mod`), µg/m³.

### Road transport externalities {#sec-fi-roadext}

The transport co-benefits module gives the cost of accidents, congestion and road damage per vehicle-km. The model turns
them into a cost per litre (or kWh) of road fuel, using the road engineer model (@sec-transport) for fuel economy and the
split between passenger and freight use ([A8.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-4)). The methodology describes these costs in
[chapter 7, section 7.2.7.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/07_Road_Transport.html#sec-extcost).

A change in fuel use comes partly from driving less and partly from more efficient vehicles. Only the driving part
changes the externalities. Its share, for road fuel $f$ (gasoline, diesel, LPG, gas, electricity), is:

$$
w_f = 1 - \frac{Q^{fre,B}_f}{Q^{cls,B}_f} \;(w_{gso} = 1), \qquad
\mu_f = \frac{\epsilon^{U}_{die} + w_f\,(\epsilon^{U}_{gso} - \epsilon^{U}_{die})}
{\epsilon^{U}_{die} + \epsilon^{F}_{die} + w_f\,(\epsilon^{U}_{gso} + \epsilon^{F}_{gso} - \epsilon^{U}_{die} - \epsilon^{F}_{die})}
$$ {#eq-fi-mrg}

where

- $Q^{cls}_f$ is the road fuel use of the vehicle classes of the fuel (`tran.cls`: passenger and freight; gasoline:
  passenger and two-three wheelers; electricity: all three), bn litres or kWh, and $Q^{fre}_f$ its freight part;
- $w_f$ is the passenger weight of the fuel in the baseline (`tran.wcl`);
- $\epsilon^{U}$, $\epsilon^{F}$ are the road usage and efficiency elasticities of gasoline and diesel;
- $\mu_f$ is the driving share of the response (`tran.mrg`), 0 where the baseline class use is 0.

The cost per unit of fuel, for each kind of externality:

$$
\begin{aligned}
acc_f &= a^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f && \text{accidents }(\texttt{tran.acc.cost})\\
con_f &= k^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f && \text{congestion }(\texttt{tran.con.cost})\\
rdm_f &= r^{km}\;\overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\phi_f\;\rho_f && \text{road damage, not gasoline }(\texttt{tran.rdm.cost})
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fi-trcost}

where

- $a^{km}$, $k^{km}$, $r^{km}$ are the accident, congestion and road-damage costs per vehicle-km of the module
  (`tran.acc.km`, `tran.con.km`, `tran.rdm.km`), USD/km; road damage is per freight vehicle-km;
- $\overline{fe}_f$ is the average fuel economy of the stock (`trafg`, `trafo`, `trafe`), km per litre or kWh;
- $\phi_f = Q^{fre}_f / Q^{cls}_f$ is the freight share of the scenario (`tran.fsh`);
- $\rho_f$ is the road share of the fuel's total use (`tran.rsh`; electricity: road demand over total demand);
- the costs are in USD per litre (USD per kWh for electricity).

Per GJ, for gasoline, diesel and LPG, divide by the GJ per litre (`tran.acc.gj`, `tran.con.gj`, `tran.rdm.gj`). The
**total road externality excluding climate**, USD/GJ (`tot.ext`):

$$
ext_{gso} = ap^{gj}_{gso} + acc^{gj}_{gso} + con^{gj}_{gso}, \qquad
ext_{die} = ap^{gj}_{die} + acc^{gj}_{die} + con^{gj}_{die} + rdm^{gj}_{die}
$$ {#eq-fi-totext}

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: air pollution and road transport externalities"}
```
for t in years:
    # air pollution cost per unit, weighted by this year's fuel use
    # cost rows: coal, gas x ind, res, pow; gso, die, lpg, ker; oop x pow, ind
    for (S, f, subsectors) in cost_rows:
        u = gj_per_unit[f] if S == 'all' else 1.0
        if subsectors is None:                           # power: the plant's own value
            cost = airpol_mc['pow', f, t]
        else:
            w = sum(ener[f, s, t] for s in subsectors)
            if w > 0:
                cost = sum(airpol_mc[s, f, t] * ener[f, s, t] for s in subsectors) / w
            else:
                cost = mean(airpol_mc[s, f, t] for s in subsectors)
        airpol_cost[S, f, t] = cost * u
        airpol_cost_gj[S, f, t] = cost
    coal_res_on = fuq['bld', 'coa', t] > ApCoalResMin * ener['bld', 'all', t]
    airpol_cost_gj['res', 'coa', t] *= coal_res_on
    for m in sources:                           # cpp, gpp, opp, rod, gro, oth, foo
        pm2[m, t] = sum(aps[m, p, t] * kappa[m, p] for p in pollutants) * T_PER_KT
    pm2['mod', t] = sum(pm2[m, t] for m in sources)

    # road transport externalities per unit of fuel
    for f in ['gso', 'die', 'lpg', 'nga', 'ecy']:
        cls0, fre0 = baseline.class_use[f, t], baseline.freight_use[f, t]
        wcl = 1.0 if f == 'gso' else 1 - safe_div(fre0, cls0)
        num = eU['die'] + wcl * (eU['gso'] - eU['die'])
        den = eU['die'] + eF['die'] \
              + wcl * (eU['gso'] + eF['gso'] - eU['die'] - eF['die'])
        mrg = 0.0 if cls0 == 0 else num / den
        fsh = safe_div(freight_use[f, t], class_use[f, t])
        acc_cost[f, t] = acc_km[t] * avg_fe[f, t] * mrg * road_share[f, t]
        con_cost[f, t] = con_km[t] * avg_fe[f, t] * mrg * road_share[f, t]
        if f != 'gso':
            rdm_cost[f, t] = rdm_km[t] * avg_fe[f, t] * mrg * fsh * road_share[f, t]
    tot_ext['gso', t] = airpol_cost_gj['all', 'gso', t] \
                        + (acc_cost['gso', t] + con_cost['gso', t]) / gj['gso']
    tot_ext['die', t] = airpol_cost_gj['all', 'die', t] \
                        + (acc_cost['die', t] + con_cost['die', t]
                           + rdm_cost['die', t]) / gj['die']
```
:::

### Welfare gains {#sec-fi-welfare-gains}

The national welfare gain adds the climate damages avoided at the national SCC, the air pollution and road transport
co-benefits, and subtracts the efficiency costs ([A8.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-5),
[methodology 3.7.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#monetized-welfare-benefits)).

**Air pollution.** The value of a change in modelled PM2.5:

$$
W^{air} = v^{PM}\,\left(PM^{B} - PM\right)
$$ {#eq-fi-welair}

where $v^{PM}$ is the value of averted modelled ambient PM2.5 (`air.vpm`), USD bn per µg/m³, from the air pollution
module.

**Road transport.** The per-km costs times the change in vehicle-km of the road engineer model:

$$
W^{acc} = a^{km}\,(VKT^{B} - VKT), \qquad W^{con} = k^{km}\,(VKT^{B} - VKT), \qquad W^{rdm} = r^{km}\,(VKT^{fre,B} - VKT^{fre})
$$ {#eq-fi-welrod}

where $VKT$ is total road vehicle-km (`trkmt`) and $VKT^{fre}$ freight vehicle-km (`trkmf`), bn km, from the road
engineer model whatever road model is selected (@sec-transport).

**National welfare gain**, the summary row of section 18:

$$
W = W^{cli,nat} + W^{air} + W^{acc} + W^{con} + W^{rdm} - EC - MC
$$ {#eq-fi-wel}

and its parts as shares of baseline real GDP:

| Row | Content | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| `wel.usd` | National welfare gain, USD bn | @eq-fi-wel |
| `wel.pct` | Same, share of GDP | $W / Y^{0}$ |
| `wel.cli` | Climate, share of GDP | $W^{cli,nat} / Y^{0}$ |
| `wel.air.usd`, `wel.air.pct` | Air pollution | @eq-fi-welair; $W^{air} / Y^{0}$ |
| `wel.rod.aci`, `.con`, `.dmg`; `wel.rod.pct` | Accidents, congestion, road damage | @eq-fi-welrod; their sum over $Y^{0}$ |
| `wel.eff` | Efficiency costs, share of GDP | $(EC + MC) / Y^{0}$ |

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: climate damages, efficiency costs and welfare"}
```
for t in years:
    for x in ['nat', 'glo']:
        dmg[x, t]  = scc[x, t] * ghg_excl_lulucf[t] / M_PER_BN
        wcli[x, t] = baseline.dmg[x, t] - dmg[x, t]

    for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'gso', 'die', 'lpg', 'ker', 'jfu', 'oop', 'bio']:
        tax = rfu[f, t] + (rfg[f, t] if f in ('coa', 'nga', 'oop', 'bio') else 0.0)
        wdg[f, t] = safe_div(tax, ener['all', f, t])
        eff[f, t] = -(wdg[f, t] + baseline.wdg[f, t]) / 2 * echg[f, t] / M_PER_BN
    wdg['ecy', t] = safe_div(rfu['ecy', t], eldem[t])
    d_ecy = eldem[t] - baseline.eldem[t]
    eff['ecy', t] = -(wdg['ecy', t] + baseline.wdg['ecy', t]) / 2 * d_ecy / M_PER_BN
    eff_all = sum(eff[f, t] for f in fuels + ['ecy'])

    for j in methane_sources:
        fee = mfee[t] * gwp[j] * fee_applies[j]
        cap = a[j] ** (-1 / b[j]) if b[j] != 0 else fee     # no cap where b = 0
        mfp[j, t] = 0.0 if a[j] == 0 else min(fee, cap)
        unabated = safe_div(em0[j] * ch4_act[j, t], act0[j])
        mfc[j, t] = unabated * ch4_abt[j, t] * mfp[j, t] * b[j] / (1 + b[j]) / MILLION
    mfc_all = sum(mfc[j, t] for j in methane_sources)

    wel_air = air_vpm[t] * (baseline.pm2['mod', t] - pm2['mod', t])
    dkm = baseline.trkmt[t] - trkmt[t]
    dkm_fre = baseline.trkmf[t] - trkmf[t]
    wel_rod = acc_km[t] * dkm + con_km[t] * dkm + rdm_km[t] * dkm_fre
    wel_usd[t] = wcli['nat', t] + wel_air + wel_rod - eff_all - mfc_all
    wel_pct[t] = safe_div(wel_usd[t], gdp_usd[t])
```
:::

### Benefits of fossil fuel subsidy reform {#sec-fi-ffs}

A second welfare measure, kept separate from the national welfare gain, values the environmental gain of the change in
fossil fuel use at the global climate cost plus the local costs (a Harberger rectangle,
[methodology 3.7.1.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#co-benefits)). For each of 16 lines $j$:

$$
B^{ffs}_j = -\left(cc^{glo}_{f(j)} + ext_j\right)\;\Delta q_j\;\frac{\theta}{M}, \qquad
W^{ffs} = \sum_j B^{ffs}_j - EC - MC
$$ {#eq-fi-ffs}

where $q_j$ is the fuel use of the line (`ffs.q`), ktoe, $ext_j$ its local external cost per GJ, and $B^{ffs}_j$ is
`env.ffs.cost` (USD bn); $W^{ffs}$ is `wel.ffs`.

| Line | Quantity $q_j$ | Climate fuel | Local cost $ext_j$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| coal, gas × industry | industry use | coal, gas | `airpol.cost.gj` industry |
| coal, gas × residential | buildings use | coal, gas | `airpol.cost.gj` residential |
| coal, gas × power | power fuel use | coal, gas | `airpol.cost.gj` power |
| gasoline, road | transport use | gasoline | `tot.ext` gasoline |
| diesel, road | transport use | diesel | `tot.ext` diesel |
| LPG | total use | LPG | `airpol.cost.gj` LPG |
| kerosene | total use of kerosene and jet fuel | kerosene | `airpol.cost.gj` kerosene |
| other oil, power | power fuel use | other oil | `airpol.cost.gj` other oil, power |
| other oil, industry | industry use of other oil and diesel | other oil | `airpol.cost.gj` other oil, industry |
| coal, gas, other | transport and other energy use | coal, gas | `airpol.cost.gj` "other" average |
| gasoline, other | total use less transport | gasoline | `airpol.cost.gj` gasoline |
| diesel, other | diesel in buildings and other energy, other oil in transport, buildings and other energy | other oil | `airpol.cost.gj` `odo` |

### Fossil fuel subsidies {#sec-fi-subsidies}

Explicit subsidies are the gap between the supply cost and the retail price, where users pay less than supply costs.
Implicit subsidies are the further gap up to the efficient price: the supply cost plus external costs plus the VAT
consumers would pay on both ([A8.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A8-6)). They are computed for 16 lines $j$: gasoline,
diesel, LPG, kerosene and other oil products; gas and coal for industry, residential, power and "other"; electricity for
industry, residential and "other".

$$
p^{*}_j = sc_j + ext_j + vat_j, \qquad vat_j = (sc_j + ext_j)\;\eta_j\;\bar{v}_t
$$ {#eq-fi-effprice}

$$
S^{exp}_j = \max(0,\ sc_j - p_j)\;\frac{Q_j}{M}, \qquad
S^{imp}_j = \mathbb{1}[p_j \le p^{*}_j]\;\left(p^{*}_j - \max(p_j, sc_j)\right)\frac{Q_j}{M}
$$ {#eq-fi-subs}

where

- $sc_j$ is the supply cost of the scenario (`supcost`: `sp`; electricity `spe`), USD/GJ or USD/kWh;
- $ext_j$ is the external cost (`extcost`): global climate cost plus `tot.ext` for gasoline and diesel; plus the air
  pollution cost for LPG, kerosene, other oil products (the `oop.avg` average) and coal and gas lines; 0 for
  electricity;
- $\eta_j$ is the VAT base flag: the household share of the oil product for gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene, 1 for
  residential lines, 0 for other oil products, industry and power;
- $\bar{v}_t$ is the general VAT rate of the year (`vatgen`): the WEO VAT rate up to the last historical price year,
  then held;
- $p_j$ is the retail price of the scenario (`rpsub`: `rpn`; electricity `rp`);
- $Q_j$ is consumption (`con`), PJ (GWh for electricity): total use for oil products (kerosene with jet fuel), sector
  use for coal and gas (residential = buildings; power = power fuel use; other = transport and other energy use),
  electricity demand of industry, buildings, and transport with other energy use;
- the "other" lines of coal, gas and electricity take the consumption-weighted averages of $sc$, $ext$, $vat$ and $p$
  of the lines above them (the plain average where consumption is 0);
- $S^{exp}$, $S^{imp}$ are the explicit and implicit subsidies (`expsub.con`, `impsub.con`), USD bn; their totals are
  also given as shares of GDP (`expsubgdp.con`, `impsubgdp.con`).

### Efficient prices {#sec-fi-efficient}

The efficient price of a fuel is what it would cost with every externality priced: the supply cost, the Pigouvian
taxes (air pollution, climate, road transport) and VAT. The tax gap compares it with the retail price
([methodology 3.7.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#energy-externalities-costs)). It is computed per
price unit (USD per litre for oil products, USD/GJ for coal and gas, USD/kWh for electricity) for 12 price codes $c$:
gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene; coal and gas for industry, residential and power; electricity for industry and
residential.

$$
pig_c = ap_c + cd_c + acc_c + con_c + rdm_c
$$ {#eq-fi-pig}

$$
p^{eff}_c = sc^{B}_c\,u_c + pig_c + \left(sc^{B}_c\,u_c + \chi\,pig_c\right)\eta_c\,\bar{v}_t, \qquad
tg_c = p_c\,u_c - p^{eff}_c
$$ {#eq-fi-effp}

where

- $ap_c$ is the air pollution cost (`airpol.cost.s`): `airpol.cost` for oil products, `airpol.cost.gj` for coal and gas,
  and for electricity the baseline value of the generation-weighted cost $\sum_k ap^{gj}_{pow,k} G_k / G^{tot}$ converted
  to USD/kWh (`airpol.ecy.g`);
- $cd_c$ is the climate damage per unit at the national SCC (`scc.cost` = `cc.code` = $SCC^{nat}\,EF_c\,u_c$), 0 for
  electricity;
- $acc_c$, $con_c$ (gasoline and diesel) and $rdm_c$ (diesel) are the road externalities per litre of the scenario
  (@eq-fi-trcost); 0 for other codes;
- $sc^{B}_c$ is the baseline supply cost per GJ (electricity per kWh), $u_c$ the GJ per price unit;
- $\chi$ is 1 if `ExternalityAddVAT` = Yes (externalities are part of the VAT base), else 0; $\eta_c$ is 1 for
  consumer codes (oil products and residential), else 0;
- $p_c$ is the retail price of the scenario (`rpn`; electricity `rp`), so $p_c u_c$ is `rp.eff`;
- $pig_c$ is the Pigouvian tax (`pig`), $p^{eff}_c$ the efficient price (`eff.price`; its VAT part is `vat.cost`) and
  $tg_c$ the tax gap (`tgap`).

**Per tonne of CO2.** The Pigouvian tax and its air pollution part are also expressed per tonne of CO2, and the
baseline excise likewise:

$$
pig^{CO2}_c = pig_c\,\frac{SCC^{glo}}{cd_c}, \qquad app_c = pig^{CO2}_c\,\frac{ap_c}{pig_c}, \qquad
txo^{CO2}_c = txo^{B}_c\,u_c\,\frac{SCC^{glo}}{cd_c}
$$ {#eq-fi-pigco2}

each 0 where its denominator is 0 (and $txo^{CO2} = 0$ for electricity). The averages `pig.co2e.avg` and `app.avg`
weight the ten fossil codes by fuel use (`effp.q`: total use for oil products, kerosene with jet fuel; industry,
buildings and power use for coal and gas).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: fossil fuel subsidies and efficient prices"}
```
for t in years:
    vatgen[t] = VAT_WEO[min(t, LastHistPriceYear)]
    # subsidies, 16 lines
    for (s, f) in sub_lines_without_other:
        supcost[s, f] = spe[s, t] if f == 'ecy' else sp[s, f, t]
        extcost[s, f] = 0.0 if f == 'ecy' else cc_glo[f, t] + local_cost(s, f)
        vatext[s, f]  = (supcost[s, f] + extcost[s, f]) * vat_base(s, f) * vatgen[t]
        effprice[s, f] = supcost[s, f] + extcost[s, f] + vatext[s, f]
        rpsub[s, f]   = rp[s, t] if f == 'ecy' else rpn[s, f, t]
    for f in ['nga', 'coa', 'ecy']:             # 'oth' lines: weighted by consumption
        for var in [supcost, extcost, vatext, effprice, rpsub]:
            var['oth', f] = weighted_mean([var[s, f] for s in sectors_of(f)],
                                          weights=[con[s, f] for s in sectors_of(f)])
    for j in sub_lines:
        expsub[j] = max(0, supcost[j] - rpsub[j]) * con[j] / M_PER_BN
        gap = effprice[j] - max(rpsub[j], supcost[j])
        impsub[j] = (rpsub[j] <= effprice[j]) * gap * con[j] / M_PER_BN
    expsubgdp[t] = sum(expsub.values()) / gdp_usd[t]
    impsubgdp[t] = sum(impsub.values()) / gdp_usd[t]

    # efficient prices, 12 price codes, per price unit
    for c in price_codes:
        u = 1.0 if c.fuel == 'ecy' else gj_per_unit[c]
        sup = baseline.supply_cost[c, t] * u
        pig = airpol_cost_s[c, t] + scc_cost[c, t] + acc[c, t] + con[c, t] + rdm[c, t]
        vat = (sup + pig * (ExternalityAddVAT == 'Yes')) * consumer[c] * vatgen[t]
        eff_price[c, t] = sup + pig + vat
        tgap[c, t] = retail_price[c, t] * u - eff_price[c, t]
        pig_co2e[c, t] = safe_div(pig * scc_glo[t], scc_cost[c, t])
        app[c, t] = safe_div(pig_co2e[c, t] * airpol_cost_s[c, t], pig)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation. The SCC rows and `cc.code` are in section 1 (with the Pigouvian taxes); the settings
  `SCCTgt`, `SCCTgtYr`, `SCCGr`, `NSCCSrc`, `GSCCSrc` and the Ricke and EPA settings are on the settings rows of the
  scenario (legacy rows 17671-17677); the Ricke values on sheet SCC; the manual path on sheet Manual inputs, row 237.
  Section 17b holds the inputs from the co-benefit modules (`airpol.cost`, `fus`, `airpol.cost.gj`, `fuq`,
  `air.con.pm2`, `air.vpm`, `tran.*`), typed for Egypt on the tabs FromAirPollution and FromTransportCB (other
  countries 0). Section 18 holds the rest: `dmg`, `wcli`, `wdg`, `eff` (LAMBDA `TRAPEZOID`), `mfp` (`MFEEPRICE`),
  `mfc` (`MFEECOST`), `cc.nat`, `cc.glo`, `airpol.ecy`, `apq`, `tot.ext`, `wel`, `wel.rod`, `ffs.q`, `env.ffs.cost`,
  `wel.ffs`, `vatgen`, the subsidy block and the efficient price block.
- **CPAT Python:** SCC in `cpat_model/mitigation/policies.py`, `prepare()` (equation M1.6); the module inputs in
  `cpat_model/air_pollution/` and `cpat_model/transport_cobenefits/` (`prepare()`); section 17b in
  `cpat_model/mitigation/externalities.py`, `air()` (A8.3) and `transport()` (A8.4); section 18 in
  `cpat_model/mitigation/welfare.py`, `step()` (A8.5, A8.6).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **SCC:** all options equal legacy. The manual SCC reads Manual inputs row 237; legacy reads a path typed on Mitigation
  row 17683 (bug L103 fixed).
- **Climate damages** use GHG excluding LULUCF of section 14.
- **Efficiency costs:** legacy's trapezoid (Harberger triangle plus rectangle), rows 17636-17648. Legacy bugs not
  replicated: the LPG pre-existing tax row is empty (the LPG average tax is halved); diesel and kerosene are converted
  with the wrong factors; the coal row is offset; non-road oil is `#N/A`.
- **Methane fee cost:** legacy's integral (rows 17628-17634). Prototype bug M21 fixed: the cap divided by zero where the
  curve exponent is 0.
- **Welfare (LD81):** legacy takes `wel.air` and the road co-benefits from the Air pollution and Transport sheets' own
  runs. Here the air pollution welfare follows the model's own emissions (the module's concentration coefficients and
  value per µg/m³, issue I105) and the road co-benefits follow the road engineer model's vehicle-km (issue I100, for
  every road model). Legacy's per-fuel unit costs are average, not marginal, damages and cannot reproduce its `wel.air`
  (issue I104): the model uses marginal damages (L224). Legacy unit-cost bugs L189-L193 fixed (L192: the residential
  coal switch tested a typed total; L193: the driving share without class use).
- **Transport co-benefits (issue I111), as legacy:** margins from scenario 1, per-km costs independent of the scenario
  (congestion does not respond to the policy), welfare a rectangle, road damage only for freight; the road damage cost
  of 0.12 USD/km is not deflated. Average fuel economy of passenger and freight vehicles, as legacy.
- **Social costs, FFS and subsidies (LD82):** legacy bugs fixed: L176 (other oil products: climate cost per barrel added
  to costs per GJ), L177 (air pollution cost of electricity), L178 (other-use averages), L179 (FFS coal and gas lines
  take another sector's change in use), L180 (FFS conversion and road damage), L181-L182 (retail price of the subsidy
  lines), L183 (climate cost on gas for power), L184-L185 (VAT base of the subsidy lines), L186 (consumption of the
  lines), L187 (other-line averages), L188 (GDP of the year in the shares). Replicated issues: I107 (FFS lines value
  diesel in industry, power and "other" at oil-product costs; FFS uses the global SCC; FFS welfare is a separate measure,
  not in `wel.usd`), I108 (electricity external cost 0), I109 (VAT base). Explicit and implicit subsidies are computed
  in every scenario group with the scenario's own prices and use; legacy computes scenario 1 only (I110).
- **VAT of the year:** the general VAT rate follows the WEO rate of the year up to the last historical price year
  (prototype bug M15 fixed: the 2022 rate in every year).
- **Efficient prices (LD83):** as legacy, with the road externalities of the scenario (I118), electricity air
  pollution from the baseline generation mix (I121), electricity Pigouvian tax 0 (I119), potential VAT on the
  externalities when `ExternalityAddVAT` = Yes (I120); `txo.co2e` is 0 where the climate cost is 0 (L203).
- **Methodology.** The methodology's efficiency cost is $\tfrac{1}{2}(ncp - xcp)(F_P - F_B)$; the model uses the
  average wedge of all taxes and subsidies in the scenario and the baseline, so subsidies count too. The methodology's
  footnote says road damage is not in the welfare benefits; the model includes it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: results for Egypt"}
SCC options in 2022 (all equal legacy):

| Option | Egypt 2022, USD/tCO2 |
|---|---|
| Target-consistent | 54.8 |
| Ricke national (key `egy.2.1p5`) | 6.87 |
| Ricke global (key `wld.2.1p5`) | 462 |
| Manual | 50.0 in 2025, +4% a year |
| US EPA | 62 |

Climate damages 2022 at the national SCC: 22.9 bn USD, against legacy's 22.0, because the inventories differ slightly.

Efficiency costs, carbon tax of 20 USD, 2031: −1.25 bn USD (a gain), mostly electricity and diesel, because they are
subsidised.

Methane fee: the fee is 0 in the shipped scenarios. A test with a fee of 50 USD per tCO2e agrees with the Python
recomputation.

Welfare, carbon tax of 20 USD, 2031, climate and efficiency parts only: +3.2 bn USD (0.39% of GDP). The air pollution
and road co-benefits come on top of this.
:::
